1) the more wealthy a district, the more likely its legislator is to support decentralization, 2) the more citizens of a district trust government, the more likely their legislator is to oppose decentralization, and 3) the more electoral prospects a legislator has at the subnational rather than national level, the more likely he or she is to support decentralizaton.

(1) parties whose future electoral success is better at the sub-national than national level, (2) citizens with greater trust in government, (3) citizens with greater wealth, are more likely to support decentralization.

Decentralization is more likely to be supported in the legislatures of Latin American countries when the parties that support the policy are more likely to win elections at the subnational than national level, when citizens trust their government, and when the economy is more prosperous."
In summary, our research is concerned with
the domestic determinants of decentralization.
the determinants of decentralization in Latin America, with a focus on Colombia and Venezuela.
the determinants of support for decentralization and how the political context affects support for decentralization in the legislatures of Latin America.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the support for decentralization in Colombia and Venezuela is not a simple reflection of a party's electoral future, but rather is influenced by the level of wealth in the district and citizen's trust in the government.
political support for decentralization in Colombia and Venezuela is influenced by the electoral prospects of the deputies and their constituents, as well as the wealth of the district.
decentralization is a policy that can be supported by a wide variety of actors, and it is not a policy that is supported by only one group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
decentralization is a policy that is supported by parties that have a better chance of being elected at the local level and by those who trust their government.
the more trust citizens have in government, the more likely a deputy is to support decentralization, and the more wealthy a district, the less likely a deputy is likely to support decentralization.

decentralization in Colombia and Venezuela is supported by parties with a strong regional presence and by those who are more confident in their ability to govern and who represent wealthier districts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
while political parties are the most important actors in the process of decentralization, they are not the only ones, and that citizen support for decentralization is not a given.
the domestic political context matters for understanding variation in the support for decentralization.
the support for decentralization is more than just a function of the electoral calculus of deputies.
